title: KV bank queueing and cross-node latency scratchpad
body:
Purpose:
This is a scratchpad capturing experiments and hypotheses about bank queueing effects and cross-node NVMe/RDMA latency amplification when the KV cache is under bursty load. Goal is to converge on a small set of mitigations we can prototype in the runtime (pacing, small-admission windows, bank-aware prefetch throttles).

Background / motivation:
- We've seen a small but painful number of tail-latency incidents in multi-tenant hosts where token-serving spikes cause long KV fetch latencies (~5-50ms outliers) that correlate with NVMe/PCIe stalls and cross-node DMA retries.
- Prior KV notes covered eviction, reuse and paging heuristics; this doc focuses on how memory-bank queuing + cross-node DMA backpressure turns short-lived high-concurrency access patterns into long tails.

Key observations (from initial traces, Feb lab runs):
1) Microburst signature: 200–700 concurrent KV reads in a ~10–40ms window (from batching + many in-flight requests).
2) On affected hosts, the hardware counters showed bank_hang / memory_channel_busy spikes (NVIDIA GPU/CPU memory counters) and a corresponding NVMe queue depth increase on the backing device.
3) Cross-node mode (remote-resident KV pages on another host via RDMA/NVMe-oF) amplifies tail: median KV RTT 0.9ms -> p50 1.1ms, p95 3.2ms, p99 18–45ms in worst runs.
4) Prefetching made reuse slightly better but increased instantaneous queueing at the device unless prefetch is paced.

Hypotheses:
A) Bank-level contention causes sequentializing of requests inside the memory subsystem; when many pages map to overlapping banks, latencies multiply nonlinearly under bursts.
B) Cross-node RDMA/NVMe introduces head-of-line effects where device retries (or retransmits) cause device queue stalls that affect all tenants on the host.
C) Unbounded prefetch + aggressive eviction churn increases IOPS and generates microbursts that the device scheduler cannot smooth.

Experiment matrix (what we ran / plan to run):
- Controlled microbench: 4 hosts, 1 min runs, synthetic access pattern generator that emits Poisson bursts with configurable hotset skew and bank affinity. Measure per-page latency, device qdepth, kernel queue stalls.
- Variants: local-resident vs remote-resident; prefetch on/off; prefetch depth 1/4/8; admission window sizes (concurrency caps at runtime): 64/128/256/512; bank-aware placement vs random mapping.
- Metrics captured: per-request latency (us), NVMe qdepth, kernel-io wait times, GPU memory bank counters, CPU steal/wait, percent of requests hitting prefetch warm cache.

Summary of earliest runs (2/20 lab):
- No admission cap + aggressive prefetch (depth 8) -> p99 KV latency 48ms on remote-resident; NVMe qdepth saturated to 128 and kernel io-wait spikes.
- Admission cap 128 + prefetch depth 2 -> p99 improved to 6.2ms, device qdepth peaked ~32. Throughput lost ~7% but tail reduced dramatically.
- Bank-aware page placement (simple heuristic: spread hotset pages across channels) -> reduced p95 by ~18% in synthetic skewed hotset test.
- Pacing prefetch requests (coalesce by 2ms windows) gave similar tail reduction as admission cap with lower throughput loss.

Practical mitigations to prototype (ranked):
1) Runtime admission window (concurrency cap) per-queue that limits concurrent KV fetches per serving core. Tunable per-machine based on measured device headroom. Cheap to implement and effective in lab.
2) Prefetch pacing: instead of issuing all prefetches eagerly, group them into small time buckets (1–3ms) or token-limited batches. Keeps client-side reuse while smoothing device IO.
3) Bank-aware placement heuristics for resident allocation: when spilling/warming, try to avoid mapping many hot pages to the same bank/channel. Needs perf counters or knowledge from allocator. More invasive.
4) Cross-node backpressure detection: detect sustained device qdepth/rtt increase and fall back to smaller model variant or local-only mode. Operationally heavy but safe.

Open questions / risks:
- What is the right admission cap that balances tail reduction vs throughput for real traffic distributions? Lab has Poisson bursts but real traffic has more structure.
- Can we get reliable bank mapping info from kernels/firmware? If not, bank-aware placement may be noisy or impossible on some hardware.
- Prefetch pacing may increase cold-start latency for some sequences; need route-specific policies (e.g., latency-critical clients get lower prefetch depth).
- Multi-tenant fairness: admission caps per-tenant vs per-host; we must avoid a tenant monopolizing the admission slots.

Next experiments to run (concrete plan):
1) Run production-like traces (sampled p50/p95/seq-len distribution) through the synthetic generator with admission caps 64/128/256 and prefetch windows 0/1/3ms. Collect cost/throughput tradeoff. (Owner: Ethan) Target: 2024-03-08.
2) Prototype a lightweight prefetch-pacing shim in kv-prefetcher that groups prefetches by 2ms buckets and exposes a flag —prefetch-window-ms. Run on staging for a week. (Owner: Priya) Target: 2024-03-15.
3) Gather hardware mapping info: coordinate with infra to run a diagnostic that maps logical pages to memory channels on representative instance types. If feasible, try bank-aware allocator prototype. (Owner: Marta) Target: 2024-03-22.
4) Instrument cross-node devices to export device qdepth and kernel io-wait to the console's per-route dashboard so we can observe correlation with tail incidents in production. (Owner: Leo) Target: 2024-03-29.

Quick notes / commands used in lab:
- synthetic generator: scripts/kv-synth/generate_bursts.py --hosts 4 --burst-lambda 200 --hotset 5% --bank-skew 0.9 --duration 60s
- capture perf counters: ./bin/kv-prof --capture-counters nvlink memchan --out run-20240220.json
- qdepth probe (linux): watch -n 0.2 'cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/nr_requests; iostat -x 1 3'
- RDMA stats: ibstat / ibv_devinfo / rdma-snic counters (custom script under infra/tools/rdma/)

Notes to self (informal):
- Don't conflate eviction-induced IOPS with prefetch IOPS in telemetry—keep tags on IO requests to differentiate.
- Consider a simple per-tenant token bucket for KV fetches that ties into console quotas for predictable throttling.
- Keep experiment configs and raw traces in the experiment bucket (GCP path) with timestamps.

Conclusions so far (working):
- Smoothing bursts at the runtime level via admission caps or prefetch pacing is the highest-leverage short-term approach.
- Bank-aware allocation and cross-node fallback are medium-term strategies that may require infra/firmware collaboration.
- We should add a short runbook: when p99 KV > 10ms on remote hosts, trigger staging test with admission cap 128 and prefetch-window-ms 2 and watch p99 response.

Unresolved: need to translate lab thresholds into per-instance defaults; will iterate after the production-like trace runs.
